newsitem.title: UK: Global warming may cause dengue epidemics - study.
newsitem.headline: Global warming may cause dengue epidemics - study.

text.p: Global warming may be helping to cause epidemics of dengue fever, a mosquito-borne disease seen most often after flooding in tropical zones, researchers said on Friday.
An analysis of dengue outbreaks compared to the El Nino Southern Oscillation, a pattern of currents and weather that affects much of the world's climate, showed a clear link.

Dengue is a threat to 2.5 billion people in tropical and sub-tropical countries. South Pacific island nations are on the fringe of the zone, but since the 1970s there have been several outbreaks, including, for the first time, the more serious haemmorhagic form.
Simon Hales and colleagues at the Wellington School of Medicine in New Zealand reviewed the medical literature on dengue and analysed occurrences and outbreaks between 1970 and 1995.
They compared this to data on El Nino and its effects, which are quantified in a very complex calculation used by climatologists and known as the Southern Oscillation Index.
The correlation was clear. The higher the index, the more cases there were of dengue fever, almost without exception.

"The result is consistent with other studies and is biologically plausible, since the mosquitoes that transmit dengue are sensitive to temperature and rainfall," they wrote in a letter to the Lancet medical journal.

Other researchers have linked the El Nino Southern Oscillation with outbreaks of viral encephalitis and malaria. Global warming is believed to affect the index, and experts predict it will cause more severe weather around the world.
Dengue, also called breakbone fever, causes fever, headaches and pain in muscles and joints. It is usually over in five to six days but can occur in a haemorrhagic form with internal bleeding.

An outbreak that started after the monsoons in India has killed at least 260 people in New Delhi and another one linked to severe flooding in Vietnam's Mekong delta affected 4,000 people and killed at least nine in October.
In July the United Nations warned that millions more people in rich and poor countries could die from once purely tropical diseases such as dengue unless global warming was halted.
